sections.heading: Asking for the rest I need
sections.text: Blessed Creator, you know my body and my limits. You have not made me to keep going without end. Please give me the sleep I need tonight, the kind of rest that restores me for tomorrow’s work. If I dream, guard even that hidden place of my mind from evil, fear, and temptation. Let this night belong to you.
theological_themes: God is the Creator who knows human weakness and gives sleep as a gift.
Rest is not merely practical but received from God in trust.
Even the unconscious hours of life belong under God's holy care.

scripture_references.connection: This psalm presents sleep as a gift God gives to those he loves, not simply as the result of human effort. It supports the prayer’s request for restoring rest from God rather than anxious self-reliance.
David connects lying down and sleeping with the Lord’s protection. The verse grounds the confidence that nighttime vulnerability can be entrusted to God’s care.

sections.heading: Welcoming your Spirit into my helpless hours
sections.text: Holy Spirit, make even my sleep a place where you are present. I cannot keep watch over myself once I close my eyes, but you are not absent from me. Keep my heart near to God while I rest, and let my whole self—body, mind, and soul—remain under your holy care.
theological_themes: The Holy Spirit dwells with and guards the believer.
Human helplessness in sleep becomes a place to trust God's presence.
The believer belongs to God in body and soul.

scripture_references.connection: Paul teaches that the believer’s body is a temple of the Holy Spirit and belongs to God. This supports asking that even bodily rest be kept as a place of God's presence and ownership.

This passage describes the Spirit’s indwelling presence in those who belong to Christ. It grounds the prayer’s confidence that the Spirit remains with the believer even in weakness and bodily frailty.

sections.heading: Letting bedtime teach me how brief life is
sections.text: As I lie down tonight, teach me to remember that one day I will lie down for the last time. Let this bed remind me, without panic or denial, that my life is temporary. When I close my eyes, help me remember that one day they will close in death. Keep me ready to come into your presence. Loosen my grip on the things of this world. Help me hold my life with open hands, knowing it is a gift from you and that I must give it back when you call.
theological_themes: Daily sleep can soberly remind believers of mortality.
Life is a gift from God, not a possession to control absolutely.
Readiness for death means living before God with faith and repentance.

scripture_references.connection: Moses asks God to teach his people to number their days so they may gain wisdom. This directly supports using the nightly rhythm of lying down as a way to remember mortality and live wisely before God.

Paul says believers do not live or die to themselves but belong to the Lord in both life and death. This grounds the prayer’s desire to hold life loosely as something received from God and surrendered back to him.

sections.heading: Hoping in the life that death cannot take away
sections.text: When pain, sickness, and weakness remind me that my health is passing, do not let me cling to this life as if it were all I have. Teach me not to fear the death that will bring me into life with you. Tonight I lie down trusting that, because of Jesus, I will one day wake in your presence. Thank you for this hope. Thank you for the gospel of grace, for the gift of your Son, and for bringing me into fellowship with you—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.
theological_themes: Death is real, but for the believer it leads into life with God through Christ.
Christian hope rests on the gospel of grace and the gift of Jesus.
The believer’s salvation is fellowship with the triune God.

scripture_references.connection: Jesus identifies himself as the resurrection and the life and promises life to those who believe in him even though they die. This supports the prayer’s hope that death is not final for the believer.
Paul speaks of being away from the body and at home with the Lord, giving biblical shape to the hope of being with God after death. It supports the prayer’s confidence about waking in God's presence.
Paul’s blessing names the grace of Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit. This illuminates the prayer’s thanksgiving for grace, Jesus, and communion with the Trinity.

sections.heading: Trusting you through the fears of the night
sections.text: Please do not hold back your mercy tonight. Your hand does not get tired. Your strength does not need sleep. Your eye never closes. Help me when I am lying here helpless. Help me when my conscience brings my sin before me. Help me when dark thoughts crowd my mind, when I imagine what may go wrong, and when my own worries keep me awake. Show me again that you are the God of all grace, love, and power. You have healing for every wound, comfort for every sorrow, mercy for every sin, and peace for every restless place in me.
theological_themes: God’s watchful care continues when the believer is weak and asleep.
Night can expose guilt, fear, and anxious thoughts, all of which must be brought to God.
God’s grace, love, and power are sufficient for sin, sorrow, and distress.

scripture_references.connection: The psalm declares that the Lord who keeps his people neither slumbers nor sleeps. It directly supports the prayer’s confidence that God remains watchful while the believer is helpless at night.
John assures believers that God forgives and cleanses those who confess their sins. This grounds the request for help when conscience accuses and sin comes to mind.

Paul directs anxious believers to bring their requests to God, with the promise of God’s peace guarding them. This supports praying through nighttime fears and foreboding thoughts rather than being ruled by them.

sections.heading: Putting myself into your hands
sections.text: Father, whether I stay awake or fall asleep quickly, I give myself to you. Keep me in your care through the night. I belong to you in my waking, in my sleeping, in my living, and in my dying. Amen.
theological_themes: The believer entrusts the whole self to God in every condition.
Belonging to God gives peace in waking, sleeping, living, and dying.
Prayer ends in surrender and trust.

scripture_references.connection: The psalmist commits his spirit into God’s hand, expressing trust in God’s redeeming care. This supports the final act of entrusting oneself to God awake or asleep.
Paul says Christ died so that believers might live with him whether awake or asleep. This gives gospel grounding to the prayer’s confidence that the believer remains Christ’s in every state.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original uses sleep as a repeated reminder of death and the bed as an image of the grave. That imagery is biblically and historically grounded but may feel stark to modern readers, so it has been preserved in plain language rather than softened away.

The line about pain and suffering indicating temporary health assumes bodily decline as a reminder of mortality. This is not presented as a claim that every illness has an easily identifiable providential message, but as a general meditation on human frailty.

The original’s phrase about death introducing the believer to 'eternal youth' was rendered as life with God rather than literalized, to avoid implying a speculative physical age in the intermediate state or resurrection beyond what Scripture clearly states.
significant_interpretive_choices: The promise of sleep to God's beloved was connected primarily with Psalm 127:2, which is the likely biblical source behind the original wording.

The request that rest become a 'temple' of the Spirit’s presence was interpreted through the New Testament teaching that the believer’s body is the Spirit’s temple, not as a claim that sleep itself is a sacramental act.

The line about 'one day awaking with thee' was rendered as hope grounded in Jesus and life in God’s presence, allowing room for both the believer’s presence with the Lord after death and the final resurrection without collapsing the two into one overly specific timeline.
